items.description:
To better understand how New Orleans residents access and use flood emergency information, we conducted surveys and focus groups with residents across the city, including flood-prone neighborhoods such as the Lower 9th Ward, Hollygrove-Dixon, and New Orleans East in partnership with Emergency Legal Responders.

Three key findings emerged among residents in more flood-vulnerable communities:

  1. Trust shapes which information people use. Residents from historically marginalized communities were more likely to rely on information from trusted people and organizations than official sources for flood information compared to the broader population.
  2. Residents want neighborhood-specific information. Participants consistently expressed a need for place-based updates that reflected conditions in their own neighborhood, particularly during rapidly changing flash flood events.
  3. Risk information and protective actions are not well aligned. Residents often received alerts about hazardous conditions but little guidance on what actions they should take to protect themselves, their families, or their property.
items.snippet: A study creating community-centered flood risk information solutions for New Orleans.

items.description:
Overview

This feature service provides a collection of Sewerage and Water Board asset layers for the City of New Orleans. It brings together point, line, and polygon features that document major utility and drainage infrastructure, along with supporting attributes for location, ownership, status, construction details, and operational characteristics.

Feature Layers
  • Water Tanks — Point features representing water tank assets, including tank name, capacity, dimensions, water levels, zoning, service area, ownership, and source information.
  • Facilities — Point features for Sewerage and Water Board facilities with basic site information such as name, address, type, and comments.
  • Sewer Treatment Plants — Point features describing treatment plant assets and related site details such as basin, district, capacity, elevations, contact information, and operating status.
  • Sewer Pump Stations — Point features for sewer pump station assets with station identification, pump count, capacity, elevations, and location details.
  • Drainage Pump Stations — Point features representing drainage pump stations with structure characteristics, elevations, reconstruction information, and site contact or location details.
  • Force Mains — Line features representing force main infrastructure, with attributes for ownership, status, service area, basin, route, and length.
  • Sewer Lines — Line features representing sewer pipes and related network segments, including pipe structure, dimensions, upstream and downstream connections, material, status, basin, and route information.
  • Canals — Polygon features representing canal assets with canal identification, category, dimensions, ownership, status, service area, district, basin, and related descriptive information.
Geographic Coverage

The service covers the City of New Orleans and reflects Sewerage and Water Board infrastructure within the municipal service area.

Source and Vintage

The layers are sourced from the Sewerage and Water Board and reflect an event-era asset inventory associated with the August 5, 2017 flooding event. The service is presented as a static reference dataset.

Use Cases
  • Utility infrastructure inventory and reference
  • Drainage and wastewater system planning
  • Operational review of treatment, pumping, and conveyance assets
  • Map display and asset location lookup in GIS applications
Licensing

City of New Orleans license terms and disclaimer language apply to use of this service.

Across most of the Parish, elevation varies by only a few feet. Most of New Orleans is below sea level and/or surrounded by flood levees. As such, the entire City is at risk of flooding.  Figure 10 displays the topography of New Orleans, showing elevations below and above sea level in cross-section looking west. The map shows that the highest areas of the City border portions of the natural levee of the Mississippi River, particularly the area near the Garden District and Central Business District. The topography of New Orleans has been particularly influenced by the natural levee of the Mississippi River. With each Mississippi River flood, water spilled out of the river, depositing its sediment to raise the natural levee to an original average of 10 to 15 feet above sea level, and one to two miles in width, sloping very gently into the back swamp. In the New Orleans area today, the Mississippi River flows 10 feet to 15 feet above sea level. The map also shows that the lowest elevations of the City are located in the areas of Lakeview, Gentilly, and New Orleans East.

As a result of this minimal elevation change, when heavy rainfall events occur, water tends to pool rather than run off rapidly. Elevations below sea level combined with little slope in topography and an extensive levee system mean that rainwater cannot flow out of the Parish and must be pumped out.  The greater New Orleans metropolitan area is served by over 80 pumping stations in four Parishes (Orleans, Jefferson, St. Bernard, and Plaquemines) with a combined capacity of over 30 billion gallons per day. All stations are equipped with pumps that are either directly driven by diesel engines or by electric motors that receive their power from diesel-electric generators. New Orleans is drained by 24 pump stations with a total design capacity of 50,891 cubic feet per second. Because the river levees are higher than the lake levees, most rainwater is pumped into Lake Pontchartrain. Exceptions are the two (2) West Bank pumping stations and two (2) stations in Eastern New Orleans that pump rainwater into the Intracoastal Waterway or the Industrial Canal. Rainfall amounts of greater than 1-2 inches an hour cause flooding of 6-10 inches in some low-lying areas, particularly those shown as being below ground elevation in the above map.

items.description: Climate change doesn't raise floodwaters evenly. As hurricanes get more intense and rainfall gets heavier, the communities that had the least to do with causing climate change are often the ones who end up absorbing the worst of it. That's the climate justice issue at the center of this project: distributional injustice in flood risk, where low income, historically redlined, and predominantly Black neighborhoods face disproportionate exposure to flooding and disproportionately slow recovery afterward. Warmer oceans and heavier rainfall are intensifying nearly every type of weather event that causes flooding, from routine storms to catastrophic hurricanes (Chakraborty et al., 2019), and in recent years we've seen a real influx of stronger, more frequent hurricanes along the U.S. East Coast. The problem isn't just that disasters happen. It's that the same disaster produces completely different outcomes depending on who's standing in its path.

items.description:
New Orleans is one of the most studied cities in the context of flood risk, and for good reason. Situated within the Mississippi River Delta, much of Orleans Parish sits at or below sea level, making it uniquely and persistently vulnerable to flooding from storm surge, heavy rainfall events, and the long-term effects of land subsidence. The devastation of Hurricane Katrina in 2005 brought these vulnerabilities into sharp national focus, yet the underlying conditions that made that disaster so catastrophic remain largely intact.

Understanding flood risk in a place like New Orleans requires looking beyond simple hazard mapping. Where water is likely to go tells only part of the story. Equally important is understanding who lives in those areas, what critical services and infrastructure are at stake, and which communities have the least capacity to prepare for, respond to, and recover from flood events. Flood risk, in other words, is as much a social phenomenon as it is a physical one.

items.description:
This layer represents fractional impervious surface coverage within the City of New Orleans based on data from the National Land Cover Database (NLCD). Fractional impervious surface data estimate the percentage of each raster cell that is covered by impervious materials such as pavement, rooftops, and other developed surfaces.

Higher impervious surface values indicate areas where rainfall is less able to infiltrate into the ground, resulting in increased stormwater runoff. When viewed alongside elevation, drainage patterns, and flood zone information, this layer helps illustrate how surface conditions contribute to urban flooding risk, particularly during heavy rainfall events.

The dataset has been clipped to the City of New Orleans boundary for use in urban flooding analysis, visualization, and public-facing communication within the StoryMap.

Source: Multi-Resolution Land Characteristics (MRLC) Consortium, National Land Cover Database (NLCD)

Areas of New Orleans that are known to experience flooding during high rainfall rate events. These areas were created from FEMA Special Flood Hazard Areas and mimic the previous Ponding Areas produced by the agency. Property owners should take extra precautions in these areas and remain vigilant when the city is experiencing heavy rainfall rates.  Reconsider parking in these areas during rainy weather. Keep personal property (homes, vehicles, trailers, offices) protected by ensuring items are elevated off of the ground.

Flooding can be experienced on any street in New Orleans given an extreme rainfall event.

This map layer DOES NOT predict flooding in any part of New Orleans.

This map layer should not be used as an indicator of future flooding.

This layer is to be used as a reference for protecting property but not necessarily to determine flooding chances or insurance requirements.

The below description is a of SWMM Models and is not the direct metadata of this layer. 

From the EPA: https://www.epa.gov/water-research/storm-water-management-model-swmm

Storm Water Management Model (SWMM) is used throughout the world for planning, analysis, and design related to stormwater runoff, combined and sanitary sewers, and other drainage systems in urban areas. There are many applications for drainage systems in non-urban areas as well.

SWMM is a dynamic hydrology-hydraulic water quality simulation model. It is used for single event or long-term (continuous) simulation of runoff quantity and quality from primarily urban areas. The runoff component operates on a collection of sub-catchment areas that receive precipitation and generate runoff and pollutant loads. The routing portion transports this runoff through a system of pipes, channels, storage/treatment devices, pumps, and regulators.

SWMM tracks the quantity and quality of runoff made within each sub-catchment. It tracks the flow rate, flow depth, and quality of water in each pipe and channel during a simulation period made up of multiple time steps. SWMM 5 has been extended to model the hydrologic performance of specific types of low impact development (LID) controls. The LID controls that the user can choose to include the following green infrastructure practices:

  1. Rain gardens
  2. Bioretention cells (or bioswales)
  3. Vegetative swales
  4. Infiltration trenches
  5. Green roofs
  6. Rooftop (downspout) disconnection
  7. Rain barrels or cisterns (rainwater harvesting)
  8. Continuous permeable pavement systems

The updated model allows engineers and planners to accurately represent any combination of LID controls within a study area to determine their effectiveness in managing stormwater and combined sewer overflows.

Running under Windows, SWMM 5 provides an integrated environment for editing study area input data; running hydrologic, hydraulic and water quality simulations; and viewing the results in a variety of formats. The latter includes color-coded drainage area and conveyance system maps, time series graphs and tables, profile plots, and statistical frequency analyses. SWMM 5 was produced in a joint development effort with CDM, Inc., a global consulting, engineering, construction, and operations firm.

items.description: This report details the hazard event of Hurricane Katrina and its effects on the city of New Orleans in Louisiana. On August 29, 2005, Hurricane Katrina hit the Gulf Coast of the USA and would become one of the worst natural disasters in the country’s history. Katrina began as a complex mix of a tropical wave, the remnants of an earlier tropical depression, and an upper tropospheric trough near the Bahamas on the 23rd of August. Recorded as third most intense hurricane to hit the USA in history, as the 10m storm surge on 29 August caused by Katrina was the highest ever observed in North America. When the hurricane hit landfall as a fast-moving Category 3 storm, 85% of the Greater New Orleans flooded due to a catastrophic failure of the levee system. Of the populated areas that constitute the Greater New Orleans, 80% of Orleans Parish, 99% of St. Bernard Parish, and approximately 40% of Jefferson Parish were flooded for weeks. Physically, New Orleans and the Gulf Coast were extensively damaged, yet other factors such as society and politics also played a role in the devastation.

items.description: Climate change is increasingly reshaping the physical and social landscape of New Orleans, where environmental vulnerability is deeply rooted in historical patterns of urban development and inequality. The city is geographically positioned largely below sea level, and it is surrounded by water, which leaves it extremely exposed to a wide range of climate related hazards, including but not limited to, coastal flooding, extreme precipitation, and intensifying heat. These risks are then even more compounded by land subsidence and out of date infrastructure systems that drastically reduce the city’s capacity to manage these environmental stressors effectively. Past events, with the most notable being Hurricane Katrina, have highlighted how these vulnerabilities are capable of producing disproportionate and long term impacts.

items.description: In late August 2005, Hurricane Katrina became one of the most devastating natural disasters in United States history. Katrina is an important case because the disaster was not only caused by the storm, but also by weaknesses in the city’s infrastructure and planning. The main drivers of displacement were the destruction of homes, the failure of the levee system, and the collapse of basic services like transportation, water, and power. When the levees failed, much of the city flooded and stayed underwater for weeks. This made many homes unsafe to live in and forced over a million people to leave. Many residents could not evacuate before the storm due to limited resources, and after the storm they struggled to return because much of the housing was lost. This disaster displaced over a million people, making it one of the largest displacement events in recent U.S. history. The impacts were not evenly distributed as low-income and minority communities were affected the most. This highlights existing social inequalities. The total dollar amount of damages caused by this hurricane was recorded to be around 100 to 125 billion dollars (A&E Television Networks) and (USDC). This is equivalent to around 200 billion dollars with inflation in today's money. This story map follows the storm’s path and how its effects unfolded in New Orleans.

items.description:
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) defines resilience as “the capacity of social, economic and environmental systems to cope with a hazardous event or disturbance, responding or reorganizing in ways that maintain their essential function, identity and structure, while maintaining the capacity for adaptation, learning, and transformation” (IPCC, 2014). Moreover, vulnerability is defined as “the propensity or predisposition to be adversely affected… including the characteristics of a person or group and their situation that influence their capacity to anticipate, cope with, resist, and recover from adverse effects” (IPCC, 2012).

In urban environments such as New Orleans, climate vulnerability is shaped by the interaction of environmental hazards, including flooding and extreme rainfall, with underlying socioeconomic conditions. Identifying areas where these risks overlap is critical for developing targeted and equitable climate adaptation strategies. Green infrastructure, particularly rain gardens, has emerged as an effective approach to mitigate urban runoff, reduce flood risk, and enhance community resilience (“Soak Up the Rain: The Benefits of Green Infrastructure.”).

items.description:
Flooding as an Environmental Justice Issue

Sea level rise and coastal flooding are often discussed as environmental consequences of climate change, but their impacts are not experienced equally across societies. As oceans warm and expand, sea levels gradually rise, increasing the frequency and severity of coastal flooding, erosion, and saltwater intrusion. These physical changes threaten housing, infrastructure, drinking water systems, and local economies in coastal regions around the world. Scientific assessments show that rising seas are already increasing the probability of extreme flooding events and will continue to do so throughout this century (IPCC, 2022).

However, the consequences of sea level rise extend beyond environmental change. Flooding becomes an environmental justice issue when its impacts are shaped by social inequality. Communities with fewer economic resources, limited political power, or histories of discrimination often live in the most vulnerable coastal locations. Because of these structural conditions, they are more likely to experience repeated flooding, slower disaster recovery, and fewer opportunities for relocation or protection. In many cases, environmental hazards reinforce existing social inequities rather than affecting all populations equally (Elliott & Pais, 2006). Examining flooding through an environmental justice perspective helps reveal how climate risks intersect with differences in wealth, race, political power, and geographic location.
items.snippet: An environmental justice story about how sea level rise and coastal flooding disproportionately affect vulnerable communities in New Orleans
items.title: Flooding and Sea Level Rise in Coastal Communities

items.description:
Before Hurricane Katrina hit, the city of New Orleans remained predominantly African American reflecting the history of the Civil War. As the larger slave population was in the south, after they were freed, many stayed in the south leading way to a heavy African American population in New Orleans. Yet, "In 2019, there were nearly 100,000 fewer Black New Orleanians in the city than in 2000, accounting for a nearly six percent drop in the share of the city’s population" (Babb, N. 2021, May 5). The devastating effects of Hurricane Katrina led to the displacement of many Black families, affecting them more than any other racial group living in New Orleans.

The city of New Orleans, Louisiana is split up into different wards and quarters, creating a complex and intricate city. The 9th ward, the ward in the lower area of the city, is especially more vulnerable to hurricanes because of the low elevation level, which also consists of predominantly black individuals compared to other ethnicities making not only the 9th ward but the black community at risk. The result of this geography and demographic makes black communities becoming more at risk of the dangers hurricanes cause resulting in loss of housing, flooding, and even danger to their lives which occurred during the events of Hurricane Katrina.

items.title: The Gentrification of New Orleans, Louisiana

items.description:
The central axiom of environmental geography is that there is no such thing as a natural disaster  (Smith 2006). Indeed, while hurricanes are natural processes, the transformation of a weather event into a catastrophe is a social phenomenon. In New Orleans, the 2005 disaster was the result of a "social calculus"—a set of political and economic decisions that determined who lived and who died based on race and class  (Smith 2006). This project explores how decades of racialized neglect set the stage for the storm, and how the subsequent racialized reinvestment serves as a "second tsunami," permanently displacing the city's Black working class  (Smith 2006).

To ground this analysis geographically, this project is set in the city of New Orleans, specifically in the Lower Ninth Ward, a neighborhood that has historically been nearly two-thirds African American (Landphair 2007). Because it is situated in one of the city's lowest “bowls,” the area faced significant flood risk and endured decades of racialized neglect, with infrastructure left to decay long before the storm hit.

items.description: On August 29, 2005, Katrina devastated the Gulf Coast, notably the city of New Orleans, flooding 70% of all occupied housing units. Many academics, filmmakers, journalists, and people of various positions have explored its effects in diverse ways. One interpretation is that as climate change exacerbates, this particular event foreshadowed society’s future climate response, in practice and policy. At best Katrina was mismanaged; at worst, premeditated. Whatever the case, this racialized event has had dire effects on Black New Orleanians’ efforts to rebuild and replenish. This case study explores Katrina's specific effects on Black business ecosystems in New Orleans through the lens of commercial real estate access and Black business corridors.

items.description: Hurricane Katrina hit New Orleans and the surrounding Louisiana area August 29, 2005 and was a massively destructive storm, resulting in over 1,300 deaths and around 600 disappearances. However, what made it so devastating was not the storm itself, but a combination of New Orleans subpar infrastructure and delay of federal aid. The levees could not hold back flooding, and many people were stranded on their roofs for days before being able to evacuate or receive aid. Many people, including several prominent hip-hop artists like Lil Wayne and Kanye West, attributed this delay to the fact that New Orleans and the surrounding parishes are predominantly Black. The hip-hop community decided to take matters into their own hands, organizing benefit concerts, dedicating songs to those impacted by the storm, and raising money. In other words, they filled the gaps that governments left and showed storm victims they had not truly been forgotten. Follow our mixtape of songs, clips, and events below to learn more about how they stepped up.

items.description:
New Orleans is one of the most flood-prone cities in the United States. Due to the “bowl-like” nature of the cities topography – much of the center of the city lies below sea level, while  elevation gradually rises as you get closer to the Mississippi River – New Orleans relies heavily on networks of levees, pump stations, and drainage canals to prevent accumulation of storm water. As intense rain events become more frequent, sea levels rise, and already overwhelmed drainage infrastructure continues to age, New Orleans becomes only more susceptible to flood damage – particularly in low-lying and socially-vulnerable neighborhoods. 

This project aims to explore how the implementation of green infrastructure (GI) – a nature-based approach to stormwater management – can alleviate the dependency on pump stations, and offer a more effective and sustainable alternative to managing urban flood risk in New Orleans. Using a GIS-based suitability analysis, I have modeled potential locations within Orleans Parish that could be suitable for GI implementation (bioswales, permeable pavement, rain gardens, etc.). Due to the ongoing large-scale road repairs and replacements within the city, I have also created a map of roads that could potentially be re-outfitted with permeable pavement. The data used to create these suitability analysis layers has been sourced from the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry (ATSDR), the Louisiana Department of Transportation and Development (LADOTD), the United States Geological Survey (USGS), and City of New Orleans Open Data.
items.snippet: Suitability Analysis of Potential Locations To Implement Green Infrastructure Development

This paper seeks to show how climate change is increasing the intensity of flooding events and how the disasters associated with them fall most heavily on the most vulnerable levels of society. The case examined in this paper is that of Hurricane Katrina in New Orleans, where environmental forces, historical inequalities in housing, and inadequate infrastructure together created a crisis in which minority communities and low-income residents suffered from some of the worst and longest-lasting impacts.

While floods and hurricanes kill hundreds of thousands of people around the world every year, their impacts will continue not to be equally felt. Those already marginalized by poverty, race, disability, or lack of resources are invariably the ones paying the greatest price when disaster strikes.

items.description:
Introduction

Hurricane Katrina is one of the deadliest storms in the United States' history. It formed in the Bahamas and developed into a Category 5 hurricane but somewhat lessened in strength before landfall in the Gulf Coast region of the United States. The destruction from Hurricane Katrina was much more than the strong wind and water associated with the hurricane because of its secondary affects. The location of the affected city was lowland and protected by man-made levees. These levees failed.

Cause

The storm surge was created by the strong wind speed of the hurricane pushing the water from the ocean towards the shore, as well as the low pressure system that pushed the water level up. But the real danger posed to New Orleans was its geography, since half of its area consists of land below sea level, so there had to be some engineered solution to keep it livable.

Natural Elements Did Their Part
Infrastructures Did Not Meet Demands
Conclusion
Recommendation

Engineering Systems

The levee protection network in New Orleans was engineered and sustained by the United States Army Corps of Engineers. The levees functioned as an intended protection from the river surges in the canals, as well as from the lake in Pontchartrain. In other words, these engineered barriers failed due to the connection points and the drainage canals rather than due to environmental inequality but rather due to engineered weakness in initial designs.

Impact

After breaching the levees, about 80 percent of New Orleans was flooded. Over 1,800 deaths resulted from the disaster, in addition to displacing hundreds of thousands of New Orleans' residents. Critical infrastructures such as housing, hospitals, bridges, roads, sewage, and power distribution were threatened, leading to persistent inundation of the cities. The residents endured threats from high water levels despite having overcome the hurricane.

Response

Engineering designs moved from prevention to damage mitigation and repair. FEMA agents and other rescue personnel implemented rescue missions using boats and helicopters, repair appraisals, and inspections of the structure, as well as the installation of temporary power distribution. In the process, failure mechanisms of the levee failure were considered in the future designs by the Corps of Engineers. It can be argued that although repair took place after failure, the original problem underscores the need to integrate design with performance, especially under extreme events.

Mitigation Eff

The mitigation strategies involved the use of floodgates, evacuation plans, water pumps, and satellite analysis from NASA and NOAA, which was utilized during the occurrence. The pumping capacity was highly relied upon by the city; however, the fact that the pumps failed shows that the pumps alone couldn't secure a region prone to hydrological issues.

Lessons Learned

The most important takeaway from the above discussion is that “protective” or “safe” structures need to perform both in theory and under critical conditions. Although there have been flaws in risk assessment, reinforcement of drainage canals, and the underestimation of design requirements in the case of Hurricane Katrina, events like these have helped compare other infrastructures that, in theory, seem to be sufficient but lack when put to test.

Future Recommendations
- Building levees and floodwalls above the level of the projected storm surges rather than at or near it.
- Improve interconnections between canals and pumps to prevent system-wide short circuits when under load.

- Utilize state-of-the art materials, real-time flood warning technology, and AI-powered prediction of surges.

- Consider the geographical context before any heavy investments are made in infrastructure, understanding that large cities lying below sea level face distinct design challenges.

Reflection

The relevance of the above case can be gauged by understanding the importance of engineering in terms of human lives. Katrina was more than an architectural or hydrological phenomenon; rather, it worked as a warning signal in terms of how the failure of prevention can lead to society’s suffering. The bigger lesson in this case could be related to the fact that disasters can occur due to both nature as well as design factors when preventions go untreated.

The objective of the Risk Area Maps is to define areas at risk from coastal and riverine hazards, distinguishing significant differences in the exposure of the landscape. Data was collected from sources accurate enough to differentiate geographic areas according to the likelihood of flooding, erosion, waves and overtopping from storm or high-water events within the project area. To the extent allowed by source data, places where flood water can extend up streams and under culverts and bridges are reflected in mapping. Compiling mapping into a summary, classifying geographic areas according to differences in vulnerability. 
The following datasets were overlaid, and combined vulnerabilities were used to discriminate geographic areas into three classes: 

Extreme Risk Areas- Areas at greatest risk of frequent inundation or vulnerable to erosion were created from the overlay of the maximum extent of the following datasets to create the Extreme Risk Area: 
  • Area at or below the Ordinary High-Water Elevation (247.3ft IGLD) 
  • Coastal areas with greater than 1% chance of flooding that are also susceptible to hazards associated with storm waves. 
  • Soils in which the likelihood of flooding is likely to occur often under usual weather conditions or is expected infrequently under usual weather conditions (approximately 5 to 50 times in 100 years). 
  • Dynamic natural shoreline feature areas susceptible to flooding and erosion. 
High Risk Areas: Areas outside the Extreme Risk Area that are at a less frequent, but high risk of inundation were created from the overlay of the maximum extent of the areas upland of the boundary of the Extreme Risk Area was compiled from the following datasets: 
  • Area bounded by the 1% annual flood risk zone (FEMA A zones). 
  • Riparian Buffer Area 
Moderate Risk Areas: Areas outside the Extreme and High-Risk Areas but currently at moderate risk of inundation from infrequent events. 
  • Area bounded by the 0.2% annual risk (500 year) flood zone, where available. 
  • Area bounded by the base flood elevation plus 2 feet of vertical elevation.
  • Soils dominated by running water or formed by water-deposited sediments.

items.description:
Hurricanes are tropical natural disasters that thrive in the warm climates of the tropics, much like the world’s greatest rainforests. They are powerful weather events that draw heat from tropical waters to fuel their strength.

These storms usually begin over the ocean as a tropical wave—a low-pressure area moving through the moisture-rich tropics—which increases showers and thunderstorm activity. As the system moves westward, warm ocean air rises into the storm, creating an area of low pressure below. This draws in more air, which also rises and cools, forming clouds and thunderstorms. High in the clouds, water vapor condenses into droplets, releasing additional heat that further powers the storm.

Storms, hurricanes, and flooding have significant impacts on communities living in low-lying and historically underserved areas. Intense rainfall often overwhelms the city's aging stormwater systems, leading to street flooding, property damage, and disrupted transportation. Vulnerable populations, including low-income families and seniors, face the greatest risks due to limited resources for evacuation or recovery. These extreme weather events also strain emergency services and highlight long-standing infrastructure and environmental justice issues across the district.

items.description: This paper critically analyzes the social consequences of post-disaster reconstruction in New Orleans through the lens of the Road Home Program; the largest housing recovery program in U.S. history. Framed as a neutral aid effort relief program, the program's formulation based on pre-storm property valuations and burdensome documentation requirements systematically disenfranchised Black, low-income citizens. Undervalued homes, informal ownership practices, and restricted access to resources rendered many ineligible for adequate assistance. Drawing on political ecology and political economy frames, the study reveals that disasters like Hurricane Katrina are not strictly natural events but rather products of structural inequality and policy failure. As The Environmental Case (Layzer & Rinfret, 2019) posits, disaster relief is political by definition as it is defined by decisions reproducing and reflecting society's values. By its dismantling of recovery's racialized geography of risk and recovery, this research discloses the way that recovery planning can be a capital-accumulation tool and an instrument of spatial displacement. Doing so, it demands an equitable, redistributive process of climate adaptation one centered on historically marginalized communities, one that resists neoliberal recoveries, and one that values equity over economic necessity.

Introduction

Over the past year, the United States has experienced a striking variety of natural disasters—each unfolding in vastly different regions, yet revealing a common thread: a growing volatility in our environment. From a rare earthquake shaking the East Coast, to winter storms paralyzing the Deep South, to wildfires sweeping through Southern California and hurricanes flooding inland mountain towns, these events reflect a concerning trend.

This StoryMap explores four major disasters that occurred across the country in the last twelve months:

1. The New Jersey Earthquake (April 2024)
2. The Palisades SoCal Fire (January 2025)
3. Winter Storm Enzo in New Orleans (January 2025)
4. Hurricane Helene and its devastating floods (September 2024)

Together, they illustrate how climate change has increased the scale and unpredictability of disasters—impacting both lives and livelihoods. Through geospatial analysis and human impact data, this project aims to bring awareness to the shifting landscape of disaster risk in America and the urgent need for resilient planning and preparedness.

items.description:
Climate change is no longer a distant threat. It is reshaping our world today, particularly in America’s coastal cities. From Miami to New York, rising sea levels and increasingly intense storms are flooding streets, displacing residents, and jeopardizing local economies. These challenges highlight the urgent need for innovative solutions to protect our communities and ensure resilience in the face of environmental changes.

The Reality Of Rising Seas

Recent catastrophic hurricanes, such as Ian and Idalia, have devastated coastal communities, bringing the issue of urban resilience to the forefront. In cities like Miami, Charleston, and New Orleans, coastal flooding has become a regular event—even on sunny days. With billions of dollars in infrastructure and property at risk, and millions of lives affected, these challenges demand immediate action.

items.description: As global warming progresses, we're facing an increase of extreme weather events. The increasing number and intensity of storms has led to unprecedented flooding in coastal communities due to storm surges. Many communities worldwide who've been grappling with these challenges for decades have developed and implemented state-of-the-art storm surge protection systems. While we can take inspiration from their success to help other coastal communities fight back against this dangerous and increasingly prevalent phenomenon, we must also recognize that these solutions are not feasible or affordable to protect those most at risk in developing countries. As such, it's also important for global leaders to investigate cheaper alternatives and continue focusing on preventing further anthropogenic warming.

USACE was tasked with the design and construction of the rebuilt system, which is known as the Greater New Orleans Hurricane and Storm Damage Risk Reduction System (HSDRRS). The HSDRRS the project differed from the LPVHPP in several key ways:

Funding. Post-Katrina, Congress allocated over $14 billion dollars for flood protection in New Orleans. items.description:
Coastal Flooding

Coastal flooding, or storm surge flooding, happens when seawater floods land areas along the coast. This happens because extreme weather events such as hurricanes, typhoons, and severe storms generate strong winds and low atmospheric pressure, making sea levels rise quickly. This flooding can greatly impact and may lead to property damage, loss of life, and environmental damage. It can also impact ecosystems, infrastructure, and communities. As populations on the coast grow and climate changes coastal flooding happens more regularly. There is a need for people to move and make changes. For example, during Hurricane Katrina in 2005, the strong winds and low pressure caused a large storm surge that breached levees and flooded large parts of New Orleans. This flooding led to extensive property damage, significant loss of life, and severe environmental damage, illustrating the devastating impact of coastal flooding.

items.description:
It is not unknown that New Orleans is at high risk of climate events. Those such as flooding and large storm events are increasingly likely as the globe warms and climate changes. As well as geographical and climate disparities, socioeconomic factors changing may put more people at higher risk.

Socioeconomic factors such as race unfortunately can greatly impact one's ability to adapt to and recover from disasters. According to the Equity Profile of New Orleans, the deteriorating economy is leaving people of color behind. About 48% of African Americans live under the 200% poverty line, with 200% as the benchmark because the federal poverty line is so low. As well as this, lower-income neighborhoods are usually in more vulnerable flood plains, which may continue to be flooded and damaged, leaving people below the poverty line with nowhere to go. Poorer coastal communities may have to face the additional cost of moving further inland to avoid high flooding risks. This is the case of Isle de Jean Charles, which is where a Native American tribe was located. It is now flooding, forcing the tribe to look further inland for housing, away from their traditional land.

items.description:
As climate change causes average ocean temperatures to increase, local sea-levels will rise and storms will be more common and more severe, threatening coastal communities.1  Proper mitigation of these storm surge events is essential to protect coastal communities before large storm events occur. Communities in Orleans Parish, Louisiana are increasingly at-risk for displacement from disaster events such as Hurricane Katrina which devastated New Orleans in 2005. Orleans Parish is especially vulnerable to flooding events due to its adjacency to the coast, large variations in at-risk populations, high percentage of impervious surfaces, and proximity to pollutants emitted from industrial plants in Cancer Alley.

Vulnerability is an intersectional issue that can reflect spatial patterns, so we employed both a suitability and overlay analysis with the above parameters to determine the most vulnerable communities in the Orleans Parish of Louisiana, USA in 2020. Repeating these analyses with census data from 1990 allows us to assess how vulnerability in Orleans Parish has changed over time, the results of which are used to spatially identify potential gaps in disaster response plans by showing the relationship between current evacuation routes and vulnerable communities.

items.description:
New Orleans, being a coastal city prone to hurricanes and flooding, of course has a large risk factor when it comes to freshwater security. New Orleans gets its drinking water from the Mississippi River and other freshwater from Lake Ponchartrain. After Hurricane Katrina, not only salinity was affected, but also the level of pollutants due to the amount of flooding and runoff. In a water quality test taken after the hurricane, only about half of all water tested in both sources met quality standards (Acholonu). This means that as severe weather events such as hurricanes become more frequent, we may see more freshwater sources becoming polluted and a large decrease in drinking water.

Food is just as essential as water. After the more recent large hurricanes such as Rita and Katrina, communities have been unable to recover. Now, neighborhoods and communities are still recovering. Community gardens and centers are still unrecovered, and neighborhoods with local markets were also wiped out (Passidomo). This raises a conversation about food inequality with lower-elevation neighborhoods usually harboring those of lower income.

items.description:
It is well known that New Orleans has a large range of socioeconomic statuses within the city, but a large amount of people are below the poverty line. Those below the poverty line are less likely to recover from damage and are more likely to live in higher-risk neighborhoods. Not only socioeconomic status but also disability, language, and housing (Climate Change & Health Report). These risks often further the divide between the socioeconomic classes. As flooding and storm damage occur, those with lower incomes may be stuck in a loop of living in high-risk areas as those are usually the cheapest.

Aside from the people of New Orleans, the ecosystems in the area are also at great risk. Most of the ecosystems around the area are marshes and other biodiverse areas. The area has about 30% of the United States’ coastal wetlands (“New Orleans Wetlands”). Each climate event puts the area at risk for flooding, subsidence, and saltwater intrusion. As well as the risk of storms, the manmade dams, locks, and levees do not help the coastline. Dams and levees block sediment deposition along the coast, and block the “cycle of new wetland growth” (“Coastal Land Loss in the Mississippi River Delta”). As the wetlands are eroded, the city is at further risk, decreasing the amount of buffer land available as more storms are likely to occur in the future. There is some action being taken, though the city is struggling to find the funding amid disaster relief in recent years.

With rising sea levels, increased flood risk and the potential for mass migration from coastal locations have become more prevalent in the media. From articles revealing the extent of disappearing island communities, to articles covering the damage from hurricanes in the US south, flooding and flood risk have increased in many coastal communities as sea levels steadily rise. The city of New Orleans provides insights into the distribution of vulnerable communities and increased flood risk as a result of rising sea levels and overall climate change.

The New Orleans metropolitan area has an estimated population of over 1.2 million people, with its highest point of elevation reaching around 20 ft, and its lowest point rests at around 8 feet below sea level. In fact, more than half of the city is below sea level. From 1997 to 2019, the city experienced 69 flooding events, from coastal floods to storm surges and flash floods, exemplifying the city's need for adequate levee systems.

items.description:
Climate change and its effects become more and more present in our daily life, as the severity of extreme weather and natural disasters increase. All over the world, nature and people experience severe consequences of climate change-related events, such as droughts, excessive rainfall, powerful hurricanes and the looming danger of sea level rise. Entire countries and cities are on the verge of being wiped off the map, as the dangerous combination of a higher water level and subsidence accelerates the rise of the water.

It is no different in the United States of America, as 32 coastal cities in the USA are experiencing more and more floods with worse outcomes (Turner, 2024). One of the 32 coastal cities is New Orleans, a city notorious for having to endure severe hurricanes and other extreme weather events, and from which hurricane Katrina (2005) resulted in the most excessive damage in several vulnerable areas. Hurricanes, however, are not the only challenge, as New Orleans is exposed to a list of other threats and risks. Risks differ per city region, but eventually, they need to be mitigated to ensure a safe future for the vibrant city which New Orleans is.

items.description: Hurricane Katrina’s landfall on August 29th, 2005, in New Orleans, Louisiana highlighted the tremendous impacts of natural disasters on the environment and people. Deemed the one of the worst natural disasters in US history at its occurrence and one of the costliest at $75 Billion1 in damages to the Gulf Coast. Katrina’s destruction wasn’t entirely a result of Hurricane winds and water movement, but additionally reliant on the failure of flooding infrastructure2. Furthermore, catastrophic impacts on the natural and urban environments from flooding and hurricane force winds have reshaped the city of New Orleans1. As climate change is projected to worsen, so will natural disasters and hurricanes making it vital to understand the impacts on environments and populations in order to plan for future events and attempt to limit the spread and scale of catastrophe. The following series of analyzed remotely sensed imagery and maps aim to give insight into the environmental and demographic impacts of hurricanes to aid in the understanding and recommendation of future infrastructures, mitigation, adaptation, and response techniques.

Thromed encompassed powerful winds and intense rainfall which caused widespread flooding and destruction, particularly in New Orleans. The city is below sea level and surrounded by bodies of water, which caused a heightened risk of catastrophic flooding. The city's levees and pumps, which were used to stop it form these event, were not strong enough in the face of Katrina's strength. The failure of these defenses caused the flooding of large portions of the city, resulting in property damage, displacement of residents, and a tragic loss of life. The tropical cyclone Hurricane Katrina hit the southwest of the United States at the end of August 2005. More than 1,800 lives were claimed in the event and its aftermath. The hurricane is also the costliest natural disaster in the history of the United States. (Hurricane Katrina, 2023)

HOW IT DEVELOPED

What would later be regarded as one of the most powerful Atlantic storms ever recorded, began as a tropical depression on August 23, 2005 over the Bahamas, about 560 km east of Miami. On the 25th of August, when the storm made landfall between Miami and Fort Lauderdale, it had already developed to a category 1 Hurricane on the Saffir-Simpsons scale, correlating to windspeeds of 119-154 km/h. The storm quickly gained power upon reaching the Gulf of Mexico with its warm waters and on August 27 it was regarded as a category 3 Hurricane. Wind speeds in excess of 185 km/h were measured. On August 29, the storm, now being a category 4 hurricane, hit the Plaquemines Parish in Louisiana, about 70km southeast of New Orleans. On its path towards the northeast it made a second landfall near the mouth of the Pearl river. The hurricane triggered a storm surge of more than 8 metres that devasted homes in the coastal cities of Gulfport and Biloxi, Mississippi. (Hurricane Katrina, 2023)

items.description:
Global climate change is becoming more and more prevalent each year with the manipulation of land being one of the main causes. Converting wetlands into farmland, deforestation, constructing dams, and destroying several prairies are all examples of how the natural environment has been altered by humanity. By changing several ecosystems and decreasing biodiversity for centuries, we are now experiencing an increase of natural, mostly human-driven, disasters. This can be seen in the severity of hazardous events such as the intense Australian bushfires in 2019, more category 5 hurricanes in the Atlantic, and flooding.

Though restoration and natural resource conservation practices need to be implemented in order to mitigate human impacts, there also needs to be updated disaster relief policies and management; specifically for vulnerable communities. A vulnerable community (in the context of climate change) defined by the California Office of Planning and Research, is a community with a higher risk/sensitivity to climate change and have less capacity (and resources) to adapt and recover from climate change impacts (California 2018). An example of a vulnerable community can be seen in the event of the category 5 Hurricane Katrina in 2005. The Lower Ninth Ward community of New Orleans still has yet to fully recover 18 years later though a neighboring community, which also suffered from the hurricane (and is not considered vulnerable), has made a full recovery.

items.description: A major environmental justice issue is the uneven risk of coastal flooding from extreme weather events, which are caused and/or worsened from climate change and are disproportionately impacting certain communities (Environmental Protection Agency, 2022). This higher risk of flooding is seen in the image to the right and is a violation of distributive justice because it is impacting low-income and communities of color at a much higher rate than higher income, white communities (Tandon, 2022). The vulnerability of these communities to flood damage is also higher so not only are they more likely to flood, but they are more likely to incur significant damage from the flooding (Walker, 2012). Justice as recognition is also being violated in some cases because the damage born to these communities from flooding has been valued as less important and received a slower and weaker response by aid groups (Khanjar, 2020). This environmental justice issue has been seen after Hurricane Sandy in New York City, NY, Hurricane Harvey in Houston, TX, and Hurricane Katrina in New Orleans, LA. In all three of these cases, flooding disproportionately impacted low-income and/or communities with people of color.

Hurricane Katrina occurred early in the morning on August 29, 2005. Out of all the places affected, New Orleans got hit the hardest. Hurricane Katrina started off as a Tropical Wave that moved across the Atlantic from Africa on August 8. It then collided with a Tropical Depression late on August 22. This then turned into Tropical Storm Katrina over the Bahamas on August 24.

It's estimated that Hurricane Katrina caused over $150 billion in damages. As for deaths, Hurricane Katrina killed over 1,800 people. What made this event even more dangerous were 3 main factors. First being that the average elevation of New Orleans is ~6ft below sea level. Second being that the levees built to keep the city from flooding collapsed below their designated height. Third being failure in government response since they didn't seem to be aware of just how bad things got in the "disaster zone." As for changes in an effort to keep this from happening again, a $14 billion network of levees and floodwalls around New Orleans was built by the Army Corps of Engineers.

items.description:
This map shows a simple summary of the social vulnerability of populations in the United States. Using Census 2010 information, the map answers the question “Where are the areas of relatively greater potential impact from disaster events within the U.S.?” from the perspective of social vulnerability to hazards. In other words, all areas of the U.S. are assessed relative to each other. Local and regional assessments of social vulnerability should apply the same model to their multi-county or multi-state region. 

For emergency response planning and hazard mitigation, populations can be assessed by their vulnerability to various hazards (fire, flood, etc). Physical vulnerability refers to a population’s exposure to specific potential hazards, such as living in a designated flood plain. There are various methods for calculating the potential or real geographic extents for various types of hazards. 

Social vulnerability refers to sensitivity to this exposure due to population and housing characteristics: age, low income, disability, home value or other factors. The social vulnerability score presented in this web service is based upon a 2000 article from the Annals of the Association of American Geographers which sums the values of 8 variables as a surrogate for "social vulnerability". For example, low-income seniors may not have access to a car to simply drive away from an ongoing hazard such as a flood. A map of the flood’s extent can be overlaid on the social vulnerability layer to allow planners and responders to better understand the demographics of the people affected by the hazard. 

This map depicts social vulnerability at the block group level. A high score indicates an area is more vulnerable. This web service provides a simplistic view of social vulnerability. There are more recent methods and metrics for determining and displaying social vulnerability, including the Social Vulnerability Index (SoVI) which capture the multi-dimensional nature of social vulnerability across space. See www.sovius.org for more information on SoVI. 

The refereed journal article used to guide the creation of the model in ModelBuilder was: Cutter, S. L., J. T. Mitchell, and M. S. Scott, 2000. "Revealing the Vulnerability of People and Places: A Case Study of Georgetown County, South Carolina." Annals of the Association of American Geographers 90(4): 713-737. Additionally, a white paper used to guide creation of the model in ModelBuilder was "Handbook for Conducting a GIS-Based Hazards Assessment at the County Level" by Susan L. Cutter, Jerry T. Mitchell, and Michael S. Scott.

Off-the-shelf software and data were used to generate this index. ModelBuilder in ArcGIS 10.1 was used to connect the data sources and run the calculations required by the model.

New Orleans, Louisiana is a major city located in southeast Louisiana, along the Mississippi River. It is known for its vibrant night life and cultural richness, due its history as a melting pot of French, African, and American cultures. It has experienced many disasters, often flooding caused by hurricanes. Hurricane Katrina severely impacted New Orleans in 2005.

The 1869 map shows New Orleans as a dense riverfront trading city built around the Mississippi River, with compact streets, small businesses, and roughly 191,000 residents concentrated near the port. Housing consisted largely of low-rise structures and housing accommodations for those in the merchant occupation. Today, the same riverfront area has evolved into a modern mixed-use neighborhood with office towers, hotels, and preserved historic districts. The modern image highlights vertical growth, tourism, and transportation modernization, yet the river remains central to the city’s identity. In 2005 New Orleans, LA was devastated by Hurricane Katrina. In the months and years after, the city slowly recovered. Schools in New Orleans did not immediately open and those that did were the schools least affected by the flooding caused by Katrina. The excel document in this lab is a list of schools that were the first to open in New Orleans. The census data is from the most recent census preceding Katrina. In this activity you will geocode the addresses of the first schools to open after Katrina and related them with a subset of socio-demographic data regarding New Orleans.

Geocoding is the process of assigning location coordinates in a continuous, global reference system (latitude and longitude) to street addresses. While street addresses are an easy way to understand and make sense of locations in a local area, there are many problems in using them for distinguishing other locations in the world. Street addresses are generally considered location identifiers within a local reference system. A street address system is often discrete, meaning it is only effective for positions that fall on the street network. For this reason, the US, Canadian, and many other countries street networks have been digitized, and coordinates (lat/long, for instance) have been determined for at least the two points that define individual line segments (smallest line segments possible). In addition to the global coordinates, the street address range for each side of the street is specified for that segment of the street network. Therefore, based on the known range of street addresses and lat/long coordinates, a reasonable approximation can be made of the location of an address on the street in global coordinates can be interpolated.

items.description: New Orleans is a culture-rich city, hosting many festivals such as Mardi Gras and a unique array of music and food. Though, many are oblivious to the challenges the city faces. New Orleans was originally built on the Mississippi to act primarily as a port to transport goods up the river. Building a city on a massive river's delta poses challenges, though. The city was built on a combination of swamps, freshwater marshes, and the Pleistocene prairie terrace. (Snowden). As a result, the soil that New Orleans was built on includes a large amount of peat and clay. As streets and buildings are built over this soil, there is less chance for water penetration and holding, which compresses the soil more, potentially leading to subsidence (Rogers). As the city expands, the risk of subsidence becomes greater with increasing impermeable cover. Apart from the geological risks and features of the New Orleans area, the local climate poses some risks as well. In the Gulf of Mexico, the hurricane risk is high. Semi-recently, Hurricane Katrina hit New Orleans and resulted in devastating floods. Levees were built to prevent flooding before Katrina (Rohland). However, subsidence mixed with a heightened risk of hurricanes with climate change decreases their effectiveness.

items.description:
The sound of a second line band rolling down Bourbon Street, Mardi Gras beads swaying in the trees, or is it the smell of fresh beignets that takes you downriver to one of America's earliest colonial port cities.

300 years may seem a long time to have the same problem, but the crescent city has continued to battle the odds against the environment and the decisions of those who came before. the first French Settlers quickly discovered how little high ground the original topography contained. In the present parish of Orleans, I focused my study question to see if the structural improvements to support and expand the seawall and leave system in New Orleans Levee system, post-Katrina (2005), reduced flooding inside this oblong ring of federally funded protection.
items.snippet: 300 Years of Flooding, looking towards an uncertain future
items.title: New Orleans: An Introductory View

items.description:
The storm that would later become Hurricane Katrina surfaced on August 23, 2005, as a tropical depression over the Bahamas, approximately 350 miles (560 km) east of Miami. Over the next two days the weather system gathered strength, earning the designation Tropcial Storm Katrina, and it made landfall between Miami and Fort Lauderdale, Florida, as a category 1 hurricane—a storm that, on the Simpson, exhibits winds in the range of 74–95 miles (119–154 km) per hour. Sustained winds of 70 miles (115 km) per hour lashed the Florida peninsula, and rainfall totals of 5 inches (13 cm) were reported in some areas. The storm spent less than eight hours over land. It quickly intensified when it reached the warm waters of the Gulf of Mexico.

In New Orleans, where much of the greater metropolitan area is below sea level, federal officials initially believed that the city had “dodged the bullet.” While New Orleans had been spared a direct hit by the intense winds of the storm, the true threat was soon apparent. The levee system that held back the waters of Lake Pontchartrain and Lake Borgne had been completely overwhelmed by 10 inches (25 cm) of rain and Katrina’s storm surge. Some levees buttressing the Industrial Canal, the 17th Street Canal, and other areas were overtopped by the storm surge, and others were breached after these structures failed outright from the buildup of water pressure behind them. The area east of the Industrial Canal was the first part of the city to flood; by the afternoon of August 29, some 20 percent of the city was underwater.

items.description:
This map shows a large image of New Orleans, Louisiana on August 30, 2005. This date was the day after Hurricane Katrina hit the renowned city. It specifically shows the flooding of the New Orleans Area. The lighter the area the more extensive the flooding is. The darker an area appears means there is less flooding in that location.

The gray and white OrbView satellite image of New Orleans was used to produce the tile layer. The tile layer sits on top of the background. The background is a topographic map of New Orleans, LA, along with the surrounding cities.

The tile layer generated 19,684 tiles that have a zoom level range of 0-17.

items.description:
Climate Change has now affected nearly all corners of the Earth; however, some areas are feeling the effects more than others. Southern Louisiana, along the Gulf, has been hit with many natural disasters over the past few decades, most memorably, Hurricane Katrina.

After Katrina brutally hit the coast in 2004, New Orleans and surrounding areas have not fully recovered, and they might never be able bring back all of what was lost. More severe storms including Hurricane Harvey and Hurricane Ida have brought more torrential flooding to the area and sea level rise is another impending issue threatening the area.

Sea level rise and severe storms have now forced the First Street Foundation to label all counties on the Louisiana coast and some surrounding counties as a level 5 flood risk -- the most extreme.

Summary
This map represents the COVID-19 in New York City (NYC) in relation to median household income per neighborhood.

Theory & Methods
I wanted to determine if the COVID-19 outbreak in NYC was relational to the median household income levels. Areas of lower median household incomes are usually at a disadvantage regarding matters of public health: New Orlean's Lower Ninth Ward during Hurricane Katrina (one of the poorest areas of New Orleans being hit the hardest from the flooding of Hurricane Katrina), the Flint Water Crisis, hurricane evaluation routes, just to name a few. To do this, I added a layer "Median Household Income" to observe the COVID-19 areas of infection. Additionally, I outlined the Financial District (or Wall Street area), to observe whether or not the one of the most financially powerful areas in the world was at lower risk to infection of the virus. 

Findings
This map shows that the opposite of my theory is true. The areas hardest hit by COVID-19 are areas of high median household income, especially looking at Manhattan area (to include the Financial District).

  • Hospitals
  • Community Centers: places of large gatherings

items.description:
Overview

This feature service brings together parcel assessment, street centerline, historic resource, and land use layers used by the City and County of Santa Barbara for planning, mapping, and record maintenance. It supports operational GIS workflows related to property assessment, roadway reference, historic preservation, and housing density management.

Feature Layers

  • Street Centerlines: Line features representing roadway centerlines with street naming, directional, ownership, acceptance, and source information for address reference, routing, and transportation mapping.
  • Historic Structures and Sites: Polygon features representing historic properties and sites with property names, construction dates, significance categories, architect and architectural style details, and links to supporting documents and media.
  • Non Historic Building Outlines: Polygon building footprints associated with historic review status and administrative tracking fields for building inventory and heritage review workflows.
  • Properties with No Land Value: Parcel polygon records for properties with missing or unassigned land value information, including ownership, situs and mailing address details, assessment values, exemption information, and parcel characteristics.
  • County Assessor Parcels: County assessor parcel polygons with ownership, assessment, address, valuation, and property characteristics used for tax roll and parcel mapping reference.
  • Multi Unit Densities: Polygon areas defining multi unit residential density designations for land use and housing planning.

Geographic Coverage

The service covers the Santa Barbara area in California and reflects contributions from the County of Santa Barbara and City of Santa Barbara mapping and planning staff.

Use Cases

  • Parcel and property assessment review
  • Historic preservation and cultural resource mapping
  • Street and address reference
  • Housing and land use planning
  • Local government GIS maintenance and stewardship

Data Notes

The layers reflect authoritative municipal and county mapping sources and include creation and edit tracking fields for ongoing maintenance. Several layers indicate a 2021 update vintage.

Last Update:  2021

items.description:
I moved to NOLA around 4 years ago. I had never lived in an area with so much access to water. It was very shocking to see just how many drainage channels, water passageways, and swamps/bayous there actually were. As an archaeologist, I have an increased interest with the history of the land, and I discovered that there was a lingering danger in this area, flooding and sinking.

Research on water level rise in New Orleans has consistently shown that flooding risk is not caused by sea-level rise alone, but by a combination of rising water and land subsidence. One of the foundational studies by U.S. Geological Survey (Burkett et al., 2003) established that much of the city is sinking at rates between 5 and 10 mm per year. This study introduced the concept of “relative sea-level rise,” which combines global sea-level increase with local land subsidence. The findings suggest that, over time, this dual process could leave large portions of the city significantly below sea level, increasing long-term flood risk and dependence on levee systems.

items.description: On August 26th, 2005, a category 4 hurricane hit the city of New Orleans, wrecking homes and displacing hundreds of thousands. Downgraded to a tropical storm by the time it hit the city, Hurricane Katrina shouldn't have been able to do as much damage as it did to New Orleans neighborhoods; it was catastrophic in part because city government had failed to maintain levee systems and crumbling infrastructure in Black neighborhoods for years before the storm, increasing the risk of flood and demolition. The story of NOLA before, during, and after the hurricane is one of immense government neglect and disregard for the lives of low-income and Black residents. The disaster was worsened tenfold as all levels of government failed to respond, leaving some drowning neighborhoods and people without assistance for several days. In a prime example of what Naomi Klein terms "disaster capitalism", governments and developers worked together to push profitable gentrification agendas in affected areas, permanently displacing thousands of Black and low-income residents and changing the demographic makeup of formerly Black neighborhoods in New Orleans.

items.description: In cities, trees serve as guardians of public health and safety. Urban trees are far more than decorations; they are critical infrastructure that can make all the difference in a community, providing cleaner air, flood mitigation, cooling, and various other valuable ecological services. Tree equity refers to the fairness of these tree benefits being distributed across communities regardless of income or background. In New Orleans, data shows stark differences in equity between communities that have persisted for generations. Here, wealthier and less marginalized neighborhoods enjoy urban green spaces and tree benefits in abundance, while lower-income, more marginalized communities are subjected to concrete jungles with tree equity scores up to 60% lower than their wealthier counterparts (Tree Equity, n.d.). This disparity is not coincidental; decades of discriminatory policies have systemically underinvested in green spaces for marginalized communities. Addressing systemic issues such as historic inequities is essential in creating environments with equitable resource access.

Hurricane Katrina of August, 2005, is remembered as one of the most destructive and influential storms in United States history. The densely populated city of New Orleans, one of many areas around the Gulf Coast to face catastrophic damage, endured extreme flooding and physical destruction when several levees and other flood prevention features guarding the city broke down. Many evacuated the city and fled to far corners of the country, and a large portion of these evacuees were unable to resettle in New Orleans after the storm. Dealing with the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina involved many immense challenges, but ten years later, one can see the effects of a decade of hard work in restoring this historic city. The drainage canals of New Orleans are a unique feature of the bowl-shaped city that are much older than most people realize. The city’s first drainage canal was the Old Carondelet Canal originally excavated in 1794, by order of Spanish Governor Baron de Carondelet. It was dug by convicts and slaves and it was later enlarged to accommodate shallow draft navigation (row boats and keel boats) between the City and Lake Pontchartrain. Its name was later changed to the Basin Canal because it terminated at Basin Street, in the French Quarter. Its name was later changed to the Old Basin Canal.

 

 

-       The Orleans Canal was excavated in was excavated in 1833 to convey water from Bayou. The Turnpike Road ran along the west side of this canal.

 

-        The Upper Line/17TH St along the Orleans -Jefferson Parish boundary excavated prior to 1849 – along the upper end along the upper end of today’s 17th St Canal.

 

-       The 1853 Ponchartrain Harbor Map shows brackish water tidal influx zone the mouth of Bayou St. John, extending westward to the New Basin Canal.

 

-       The Upper Protection Canal was excavated around 1857 -58 out to Lake Ponchartrain and this became 17th street canal.

 

-       By 1863 there were a series of east-west feeder canals serving Bayou St. John from the west side

 

-       By 1863 there were a series of NNE trending drainage canals in St. Bernard Parish.
sections.title: History of canals

sections.content:
- trade canals: (florida avenue, 40 arpents) these were mainly used for commerce. American traders and farmers floated their goods downstream to New Orleans and, after 1812, steamboats transported upriver commodities that ocean-going vessels landed at New Orleans. The modern history of the Port of New Orleans, however, began in 1896 when the Louisiana state legislature created a state agency to serve as port authority.

- there also what can be called connecting canal: like the Inner Harbor Navigational Canal was built in 1925 to connect the Mississippi River and Lake Pontchartrain( Also known as the Industrial Canal) it serves as the mouth of the Mississippi River-Gulf Outlet, built in the 1960s as a route to the Gulf of Mexico that is more than forty miles shorter than the Mississippi River route.
 

- drainage canals: these are the ones that were used to pump  water out of the city. the three main are  New Orleans, the 17th street canal and London avenue canals.
sections.title: Types of canals

sections.content:
Canals in New Orleans are surrounded by levees and flood gates.

There are 13 miles (21 km) of Levees and floodwalls that line the sides of the canals.

 

The 17th Street Canal extends 13,500 feet (4,100 m) north from Pump Station 6 to  Lake Pontchartrain along the boundary of Orleans and Jefferson parishes. The Orleans Avenue Canal, between the 17th Street and London Avenue canals, runs approximately 11,000 feet (3,400 m) from Pump Station 7 to Lake Pontchartrain. The London Avenue Canal extends 15,000 feet (4,600 m) north from Pump Station 3 to Lake Pontchartrain about halfway between the Orleans Avenue Canal and the Inner Harbor navigation canal (industrial canal). here is a picture of canal.

 

One of the biggest project was the Lake Borgne Surge Barrier that was build by US Army Corp of Engineers. Here is one a video of it's construction. it cost $1.1 billion  and it took up to 4 years to be completed.

All these drainage and levee systems is described as a dilemma because although it has positive impact of solving short term problems, it continue to create long term problems.

three main levees failures are: overtopping, underseepage and breaches.
