sections.content:
Greg Miller

Bucknell in New Orleans 2015

#nolabison15

 

Since the city’s inception, the wetlands surrounding New Orleans have played a crucial role in its existence. As the city grew and adapted to the unpredictable nature of the Mississippi River, canals, levees and dams were built to control and combat flooding. However with decades of this construction, the flow of the Mississippi River sediment that sustains the wetlands has become choked off causing a major jump in the rate of wetland subsidence. “Every hour, a football field of wetlands disappear.” “According to Louisiana State geologists, approximately 5,122 square miles of coast line will be lost by 2100.” As alarming statistics circulate in the media, organizations such as the Coastal Protection and Restoration Authority have started to take action with an elaborate 50 year plan to restore the wetlands. The plan moves to divert sediment back to its natural path, which will sustain a diversity of coastal habitats including cypress swamps, marshes, barrier islands, and ridges all of which will provide protection. Not only do the wetlands provide physical protection to the city, but they also sustain some of the area’s and United States’s vital energy production, fishing and shipping industries. Additionally, with the potential disappearance of areas such as the Lower Ninth Ward and the bayous close to Gulf, the music associated with these cultures is at high risk of disappearing as well. This map moves to tell this story of the wetlands, its past evolution, its current status, plans for the future, and the related economic, cultural, and musical effects.
sections.title: The Story of Louisiana's Coastal Wetlands

sections.content:
How were the Wetlands formed?

 

 

Sediment transport and deposition: 

 

Louisiana's coastal wetlands as we know them today were formed approximately over the last 7,000 years in a process known as the delta cycle. With each stage in the cycle (~1000-2000 years), a new delta lobe is created as the Mississippi transports sediment from the interior of the continent and releases them towards the Gulf of Mexico. As this sediment builds up underwater, this builds a conducive environment for plants to grow which are sustained through the flow of organic materials constantly accumulating. 

 

However, as the delta lobe continues to build up, the path of the Mississippi in turn becomes indirect and longer. In result, the river opts to change its direction by cutting a shorter route to the Gulf, abandoing the older lobe. Because these older lobes now have no direct flow of sediment, they gradually start to erode, leaving behind barrier islands to mark their former thriving existences. 

 

But with death comes rebirth as new parts of the Gulf start to receive sediment flow, forming new lobes where trees and marsh plants can root their foundation. Given the cyclical nature of the wetlands existence, " a natural delta exists in a state of constant change." This dynamic unpredictability makes it even harder to predict the geographic location of these wetlands. 

 

As indicated by the flow chart above, the wetlands have evolved in location but more recently undergo threat from constant human activity including the construction of dams, levees, and canals: setting the scene for today's ecological struggles.
sections.title: Evolution of Wetlands

sections.content:
In 2005 with Katrina on New Orleans's doorstep, the Mississippi River Delta is already disappearing at the rate of a "football field per hour"

 

Given this extreme rate of disappearance among many other natural setbacks, the city of New Orleans was already set up for failure before Hurricane Katrina. 

 

Contributing Factors to Pre-Katrina Disaster: 

 

Levees and Canals: Ironically, perhaps one of the most significant issues facing the wetlands are the very human structures that are trying to control the river ensuring their existence. Over the years, the Mississippi River has been bombarded with levees (intended to reduce flooding), and shipping canals such as the Mississippi River- Gulf Outlet (MRGO). Unfortunately, while these strucutres had original good intent, these channels change the hydrology and the flow of water in and around the wetlands. This change in hydrology allows for saline waters from the Gulf to penetrate and ultimatly kill the vegetation of the freshwater wetlands.  

 

Oil and Gas Infrastructure: Louisiana is America's Energy Coast. With such a huge role in sustaining America's energy sources in oil, comes lots of infrastructure. There are thousands of offshore oil rigs and onshore wells, with pipelines connecting them all. With time, these human activities have directly impacted the coastal wetlands, changed the hydrology and sped up the erosion process. 

 

Dams upriver: As it is known, the sediment so crucial for the wetlands comes from flow from connecting Rivers such as the Ohio and Missouri Rivers. However, with engineering innovation such as locks and dams- valuable sediments are trapped and are unable to reach the mouth of the Mississippi.  

 

Hurricanes:

 

According to and confirmed by AIR worldwide, a national hurricane agency, New Orleans is situated in the highest risk location for Hurricane Damage given its coastal location. This was confimed by Hurricanes Katrina and Rita in 2005. 

 

 

 

Invasive species: A lesser known cause of wetlands disappearance are nutria which are fast breeding, aggresive foraging rodents originally introduced back in the 18th century for fur trade. While the economic industry was supported by this trade, their presence within the wetlands has been near disastrous. They burrow into the ground, and eat the roots of marsh plants devouring cypress seedlings. Yet another increased nuisance to the potential for wetlands to thrive. Attempts at eradicating these pests have been relatively difficult, as floating traps and poison often interfere with the delicacy of the surrounding wetlands.
sections.title: Pre-Katrina

sections.content:
Katrina hits: Now what? 

 

In the late summer of 2005, Louisiana suffered through two massive hurricanes: Hurricane Katrina in August, and Hurricane Rita in September. These storms brought unprecedented destruction and demonstrated the catastrophic impact of land loss. It confirmed the risk of New Orleans's geographic location. 

 

After Hurricane Katrina hits, Louisiana is in a state of supreme shock, but moreso realization of the importance of the wetlands. If wetlands were a greater presence, countless models scientifiaclly predict that the impacts of Katrina would have been far more manageable. In short, a far lesser reliance on the levee system would have been needed. Moreover, the remaining marshes and swamps are not as robust as they once were. The extensive wetlands that once lay to the south and east of New Orleans and protected it from storms have been threaded with oil pipeline ditches and navigation canals like the MRGO. These man-made intrusions bring salt water deep into the brackish and freshwater wetlands of southern Louisiana, disrupting the salinity balance required by the plants that hold wetland solid together. This intrusion of ocean water results in areas that appear healthy on the surface but are too weak to withstand storms of Katrina's or Rita's strength
sections.title: Post-Katrina

sections.content:
New Orleans is home to many of America's backbone industries. The wetlands remain as the main source of protection for these industries. 

 

Shipping: Ports like Baton Rouge and Lake Charles link the Mississippi and the American Midwest with the rest of the world. With five of the country's fifteen largest ports within its borders, Louisiana handles about a fifth of all water born commerce in the United States, making the star a vital conduit for foreign and domestic trade


Natural Resources:

 

Fisheries in and around coastal LA serve as an important source of seafood for much of the United States, while the wetland habitats of the Mississippi River Delta attract hundreds of thousands of hunters and fishermen each year.
 

The Mississippi Delta and Seafood:

 

 

Statistics: 

 

"More than a third of America's oysters are harvested from LA waters."

 

"Louisiana wetlands are responsible for roughly 25% of the blue crabs caught nationwide." 


"Louisiana shrimpers catch roughly a million pounds of both brown and white shrimp every year." 

 

The Mississippi River Delta's marshes and wide variety of salinities provide ideal habitat for oysters, shrimp, crabs and many species of fish. But as the delta's wetlands disappear, so does the ability to support this abundant marine life. Restoration projects that reconnect the river with its wetlands, that rebuild marsh wetlands and barrier islands will ultimately support a more abundant seafood harvest.


Economic Challenges Involved:

 

Louisiana as a state faces unique and serious economic challenges. In addition to rising unemployment over the past several years due to the recession, the cost of repairing the coast and reversing the damage from the oil spill was in the billions of dollars. However, with this disaster comes the opportunity for employment: the act of restoration itself provides economic benefits, leading to investment and new jobs throughout the entire supply chain. By promoting restoration we have the opportunity to provide jobs today and prevent larger ecological catastrophes in the future.

 

Up and coming source of economic employment: 

 

Systems such as GIS allow us to map, model, query, and analyze large quanties of data within a single database accoring to location. The employment of such technology aids especially in corporate firms such as the Coastal Authority for Wetlands Restoration, who sponors a 50 year Master Plan. Given the radical nature of unpredictable wetlands, mastery of this technology has allowed for a knowledge and understanding previously unavailable to us.
sections.title: Coastal Industries at risk

sections.content:
One of the geographic locations that would be most susceptible to wetland loss would be the land of the bayous, home to a culture with perhaps one of the most unique histories. 

 

Approximately 400 years ago, a small group of settlers left their hometown in France and sailed their way to their new home of eastern Canada. Here in Canada, they made peace with the Indians and managed to transform their once small land settlements into prosperous farm land and trading posts. The identity of these people evolved into “Acadian” who were an insignificant and innocent presence to both the King of France and British Crown. The King of France was more concerned with the Province of Quebec to the East, and the English Monarch was concerned with the colonies of New England. The Acadians not wanting any part of the French-English feud, became a devout people of neutrality. 
 
Unfortunately for the Acadians, in 1754, Major Charles Lawrence of England unjustly ordered that the Acadian people rescind their Catholic religion and join allegiance to the monarch. When the Acadians did not comply, their villages and colonies were burned down, given their inability to fight back. And so, a massive exodus would ensue. 
 
Years of wandering followed, as the Acadians were a people without a homeland. A variety of fates awaited these people: arrest in England, outcast in France, neglect in the colonies. However one ship of Acadians found its way to Louisiana, which at the time was a Spanish colony. The Spanish saw potential in these people, and more so an advantage as their presence could act as a counteraction against dangerously close British settlements. The Acadian culture grew mostly in this area of Louisiana in the bayous, swamps, and other unwanted land. Even in this new location, they continued to be rejected by the Frenchmen of Louisiana because of their strange patois. 
 
As time progressed, Acadians eventually started to marry outside their bubbled society and so the Cajun culture was born. 

 

 

 

Out of Cajun culture, we receive a rich music that evolved from its roots in the music of the French-speaking Canadian Catholics. This music is characterterized by the predominant use of the fiddle, but the genre would later give way to the accordion. The genre has gained national accclaim and in 2007 even eared its on Grammy category: "Best Zydeco or Cajun Music Album." If the wetlands recede past these bayous, the homelands of the music will be no longer, further dispersing and losing the community that bonds so strongly over this music.
sections.title: Coastal Communities at Risk: the Culture of Cajun

sections.content:
The Lower Ninth Ward and Bounce Music:

 

As of the last decade, New Orleans has its own musical geography in the genre known as bounce, which can be characterized as the local variation on hip-hop. Bounce is extremely energetic music, born out of the housing projects, the neighborhoods, and often high school areas. The housing projects that were destroyed after Hurricane Katrina and the public schools that were turned into charter schools live on in this music.

 

This energetic and rambunctious New Orleans variant of hip-hop often pays homage to the city's neighborhoods, blocks, and housing projects and is fraught with New Orleans heritage. It is charactertized by a "rip roaring call and response" theme, including a swinging beat. This dance party music aptly termed "bounce" is ubiquitous in local nightclubs, block parties, and, more than anywhere else, the city's storied housing projects.

 

 

 

This type of music is uniquely representative. Representative of where you are from, the name of your school, your neighborhood. Represent your ward is the attitude associated with this music. Represent the street. This music is highly integrative geographically speaking, putting people on the map. 

 

With receding wetlands, areas such as the Lower Ninth could suffer the most given another Katrina- like stormw which would drive the culture elsewhere geographically. Given the strong roots in the Lower Ninth, the genre could very well disintegrate without its geographic foundation.
sections.title: Coastal Communities and Culture at Risk

sections.content:
"If we're going to succeed, we're going to have to mimic nature"

 

To restore the wetlands, the Coastal Protection and Restoration Authority has constructed a 50 year 50 billion dollar "Master Plan" to divert sediment back to its natural path. 

 

This plan was released in draft form in January 2012 and passed unanimously by the Louisiana legislature in April 2012. The Coastal Master Plan builds off previous plans but is the most comprehensive attempt yet at putting forth solutions to coastal LA's myriad environmental and engineering challenges.

 

The key to this process lies in recognizing that LA's coast is changing and will continue to change while also realizing that accepting the status quo will invariably lead to continued ecological collapse and erosion of Louisiana's barrier islands and wetlands.

 

Problems:

 

1.) Sea Level Rise: Estimates of Sea Level Rise over the next 50 years fell somewhere between .27 an .65 meters due to rising air temperatures and climate change. 

 

 

 

2.) Marsh Collapse: Wetland vegetation can no longer persist and the area will rapidly lose elevation and covert from wetland to open water. 

 

General Solution: "Sustain key levee protection systems, such as Greater New Orlans area and Larose to Golden Meadow. New levees are included for large densely populated, at risk communities. Nonstructural protection measures are included for all parishes in this region. "

 

The Restoration Goal: "Use sediment and water from the Mississippi River to sustain and rebuild land. Sustain a diversity of coastal habitats including cypress swamps, marshes, barrier islands, and ridges." 

 

Types of Projects:

 

Structural Protection

Bank Stabilization

Oyster Barrier Reef

Ridge Restoration 

Shoreline Protection

Barrier Island Restoration

Marsh Creation

Sediment Diversion

Hydrologic Restoration 

 

*** Noteworthy plan: Lake Pontchartrain Barrier: Planning, engineering and design to construct a levee to an elevation of 24.5 feet across the mouth of Lake Pontchartrain from the New Orleans Landbridge to Interstate 59 for hurricane storm surge risk reduction.

 

2017 Update: Improvements and concentration on nonstructural organziation: refining policies to help communities communicate, and better understnad flood policies.
